text: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 5 seconds. Find its final velocity.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The car moves with constant (uniform) acceleration starting from rest, so the standard equations of motion apply.
Select v = u + at to relate final velocity to initial velocity, acceleration, and time.
Substitute u = 0, a = 2 m/s², t = 5 s: v = 0 + 2 × 5.
Compute v = 10 m/s, matching the option 10 m/s.

20 m/s.misconception: used v = 2at instead of v = u + at, effectively doubling the product a×t

7 m/s.misconception: added a and t (2 + 5) instead of multiplying them

5 m/s.misconception: divided the product at by 2, confusing it with an average-velocity style formula

text: A car moving at 10 m/s applies its brakes, producing a uniform deceleration of 2 m/s². Find the distance it travels before coming to rest.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The car decelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to rest, so the kinematic equation linking v, u, a, and s applies.
Select v² = u² − 2as, with final velocity v = 0.
Rearrange to s = u²/(2a) and substitute u = 10 m/s, a = 2 m/s²: s = 100/(2×2).
Compute s = 100/4 = 25 m.

50 m.misconception: dropped the factor of 2 in the denominator, computing s = u²/a instead of u²/(2a)

5 m.misconception: used the linear relation s = u/a instead of the correct s = u²/(2a)

20 m.misconception: arithmetic slip while dividing 100 by 4, incorrectly getting 20 instead of 25

text: A particle starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 4 m/s² for 3 seconds. It then decelerates uniformly at 3 m/s² until it comes to rest. Find the total distance covered by the particle.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The motion has two distinct phases — uniform acceleration followed by uniform deceleration — so each must be analyzed separately and the distances added.
For phase 1 use v = u + at and s = ut + ½at²; for phase 2 use v² = u² − 2as with the phase-1 final velocity as the new initial velocity.
solution_steps.formula_used: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² − 2as
v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² − 2as

solution_steps.step_text: Total distance = s₁ + s₂ = 18 + 24 = 42 m.

18 m.misconception: computed only the acceleration-phase distance and forgot to add the deceleration-phase distance

24 m.misconception: computed only the deceleration-phase distance and forgot to add the acceleration-phase distance

66 m.misconception: for phase 2, dropped the factor of ½ implicit in v²=2as and instead used s₂ = v×t (12×4=48), giving an inflated total

text: A ball is projected horizontally from the top of a tower of height 45 m with a speed of 15 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the time it takes to hit the ground.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The horizontal launch speed does not affect the time of flight; only the vertical fall under gravity determines it.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying independence of horizontal and vertical motion

solution_steps.step_text: Select h = ½gt² for the vertical fall, and solve for t.
Substitute h = 45 m, g = 10 m/s²: t² = 2×45/10 = 9.
Take the square root: t = √9 = 3 s.

9 s.misconception: computed 2h/g = 9 correctly but forgot to take the square root

4.5 s.misconception: used t = h/g, omitting the factor of 2 entirely instead of t = √(2h/g)

1.5 s.misconception: divided the correct answer by 2, incorrectly assuming a half-time symmetry rule

text: A ball is projected with a speed of 20 m/s at an angle of 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², sin 30° = 0.5, find the maximum height reached.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: Maximum height in projectile motion depends only on the vertical component of the initial velocity.
Select H = u²sin²θ/(2g).
Substitute u = 20 m/s, sin30° = 0.5 so sin²30° = 0.25, g = 10 m/s²: H = 400×0.25/20.
Compute H = 100/20 = 5 m.

10 m.misconception: used sinθ (0.5) instead of sin²θ (0.25) in the height formula

20 m.misconception: omitted the sin²θ factor entirely, effectively computing H = u²/(2g)

2.5 m.misconception: arithmetic slip, computing sin²30° as 0.125 instead of 0.25

text: A projectile is launched from level ground with a speed of 50 m/s at an angle of 37° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8, find its horizontal range.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: For a projectile launched and landing at the same height, the standard range formula applies.
Select R = u²sin2θ/g, where sin2θ = 2sinθcosθ.
Compute R = 2400/10 = 240 m.

120 m.misconception: dropped the factor of 2 in sin2θ = 2sinθcosθ, effectively computing R = u²sinθcosθ/g

90 m.misconception: used sin²θ in place of sin2θ

45 m.misconception: computed the maximum-height formula instead of the range formula

text: A horizontal force of 20 N is applied to a 5 kg block resting on a frictionless surface. Find the resulting acceleration.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: With no friction, the net force on the block equals the applied force, so Newton's second law applies directly.
Select a = F/m.
Substitute F = 20 N, m = 5 kg: a = 20/5.
Compute a = 4 m/s².

100 m/s².misconception: multiplied force and mass instead of dividing (20×5)

0.25 m/s².misconception: inverted the formula, computing m/F instead of F/m

15 m/s².misconception: subtracted mass from force (20 − 5) instead of dividing

text: Two blocks of mass 2 kg and 3 kg are connected by a light string over a frictionless pulley (an Atwood machine). Taking g = 10 m/s², find the acceleration of the system.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The heavier mass falls, pulling the lighter mass up; the whole system shares one common acceleration.
Select a = (m2 − m1)g/(m1 + m2), where m2 > m1.
Compute a = 2 m/s².

10 m/s².misconception: forgot to divide by the total mass (m1+m2), stopping at (m2−m1)g

5 m/s².misconception: divided by the lighter mass m1 alone instead of the total mass m1+m2

0.5 m/s².misconception: inverted the acceleration formula, computing (m1+m2)/[(m2−m1)g] instead

text: A 4 kg block rests on a frictionless incline of angle 30° and is connected by a string over a pulley at the top of the incline to a 6 kg mass hanging vertically. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the acceleration of the system.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The hanging mass's weight drives the system, opposed by the component of the incline block's weight along the incline (m1g sinθ).
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying forces along the incline and string

solution_steps.step_text: Select a = (m2g − m1g sinθ)/(m1 + m2), from combining Newton's second law for both masses.
Compute a = 4 m/s².

10 m/s².misconception: divided the net force by m1 alone instead of the total mass (m1+m2)

2 m/s².misconception: forgot the sinθ factor, treating the full weight m1g as resisting the motion instead of its component along the incline

5 m/s².misconception: used sin²θ instead of sinθ for the incline component

text: A 4 kg block rests on a horizontal surface. The coefficient of friction between the block and surface is 0.5. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the maximum static friction force.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The maximum static friction force depends on the normal reaction and the coefficient of friction.
Select f = μmg, since the surface is horizontal so the normal force equals mg.
Substitute μ = 0.5, m = 4 kg, g = 10 m/s²: f = 0.5 × 4 × 10.
Compute f = 20 N.

40 N.misconception: computed only mg, forgetting to multiply by the coefficient of friction μ

80 N.misconception: divided mg by μ instead of multiplying by μ

2 N.misconception: computed μm but forgot to include g

text: A 5 kg block is pulled by a horizontal force of 25 N on a surface with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the block's acceleration.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The block experiences the applied force and an opposing kinetic friction force, so the net force drives the acceleration.
Select friction f = μmg, and net force F_net = F − f, then a = F_net/m.
Substitute μ = 0.3, m = 5 kg, g = 10 m/s²: f = 0.3×5×10 = 15 N. Net force = 25 − 15 = 10 N.
Compute a = 10/5 = 2 m/s².

5 m/s².misconception: ignored friction entirely, computing a = F/m

10 m/s².misconception: correctly found the net force (10 N) but forgot to divide by the mass

8 m/s².misconception: sign error — added the friction force to the applied force instead of subtracting it

text: A constant force of 10 N acts on a body, producing a displacement of 5 m in the direction of the force. Find the work done.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: Since the force and displacement are in the same direction, work is simply their product.
Select W = F × d.
Substitute F = 10 N, d = 5 m: W = 10 × 5.
Compute W = 50 J.

2 J.misconception: divided force by displacement instead of multiplying

15 J.misconception: added force and displacement instead of multiplying them

0.5 J.misconception: divided displacement by force, inverting the formula

text: A 2 kg block moving at 4 m/s is brought to rest by a constant friction force acting over a distance of 4 m. Use the work-energy theorem to find the friction force.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The block's entire kinetic energy is removed by the work done against friction.
Select KE = ½mv², and equate it to the work done by friction, f×d.
Substitute m = 2 kg, v = 4 m/s, d = 4 m: ½×2×16 = f×4, so 16 = 4f.
Compute f = 16/4 = 4 N.

8 N.misconception: dropped the factor of ½ in KE=½mv², using KE=mv² instead

2 N.misconception: used momentum mv instead of kinetic energy ½mv²

16 N.misconception: computed the kinetic energy correctly (16 J) but forgot to divide by the distance

text: A 1 kg block slides down a frictionless incline from a height of 5 m and then moves along a rough horizontal surface with coefficient of friction 0.2. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the distance it travels on the horizontal surface before stopping.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The gravitational potential energy at the top converts entirely into kinetic energy at the bottom, which is then dissipated entirely by friction on the horizontal surface.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying the energy conservation and dissipation scenario

solution_steps.step_text: Equate mgh to the work done against friction, μmg × d.
Substitute h = 5 m, μ = 0.2, g = 10 m/s² (mass cancels): 10×5 = 0.2×10×d, so 50 = 2d.
Compute d = 50/2 = 25 m.

5 m.misconception: assumed the sliding distance equals the incline height, ignoring the energy-friction balance entirely

10 m.misconception: used μ = 0.5 instead of the given 0.2

2.5 m.misconception: left out g in the energy term, using mh instead of mgh

text: A 3 kg object moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg object and sticks to it. Find the velocity of the combined mass immediately after the collision.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: This is a perfectly inelastic collision, so total momentum is conserved and the two masses move together afterward.
Select m1v1 = (m1+m2)v.
Substitute m1 = 3 kg, v1 = 4 m/s, m2 = 1 kg: 3×4 = (3+1)×v, so 12 = 4v.
Compute v = 12/4 = 3 m/s.

12 m/s.misconception: computed the total momentum correctly (12 kg·m/s) but forgot to divide by the combined mass

4 m/s.misconception: assumed the moving object's velocity is unchanged after sticking to the stationary one

6 m/s.misconception: used the difference of the masses (m1−m2) instead of their sum in the denominator

text: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on elastically with a stationary 2 kg ball. Find the velocity of the first ball (the initially moving one) immediately after the collision.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: This is a perfectly elastic head-on collision between two equal masses, one initially at rest.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying an elastic collision between equal masses

solution_steps.step_text: For an elastic collision between equal masses with one at rest, the velocities are exchanged: the moving ball stops and the stationary ball takes on its velocity.
Substitute m1 = m2 = 2 kg into v1' = [(m1−m2)/(m1+m2)]v1 = [(2−2)/4]×6.
Compute v1' = 0 m/s.

6 m/s.misconception: assumed the first ball keeps its original velocity, not realizing that equal masses in an elastic collision exchange velocities entirely

3 m/s.misconception: averaged the two velocities as if the collision were perfectly inelastic (bodies moving together)

12 m/s.misconception: added the velocities together instead of applying the elastic-collision exchange rule

text: A bullet of mass 0.02 kg moving at 300 m/s embeds itself in a stationary wooden block of mass 1.98 kg. Find the percentage of the initial kinetic energy lost in this perfectly inelastic collision.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: This is a perfectly inelastic collision; momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not, so both the initial and final KE must be found and compared.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying energy loss in an inelastic collision

solution_steps.step_text: Find the common velocity from momentum conservation, m1v1 = (m1+m2)v, then compute KE_initial = ½m1v1² and KE_final = ½(m1+m2)v².
Substitute m1 = 0.02 kg, v1 = 300 m/s, total mass = 2 kg: v = 0.02×300/2 = 3 m/s. KE_initial = ½×0.02×300² = 900 J. KE_final = ½×2×3² = 9 J.
Fraction lost = (900−9)/900 = 891/900 ≈ 0.99, i.e. 99% of the kinetic energy is lost.

1%.misconception: computed the fraction of energy retained rather than the fraction lost, reporting (1 − fraction lost) instead

50%.misconception: assumed a generic 'half the energy is lost' rule for inelastic collisions instead of computing it from the actual masses and speed

100%.misconception: used only the bullet's mass instead of the combined mass when computing the final kinetic energy, making it look like essentially all the KE vanished

text: A car moves in a circular path of radius 25 m with a constant speed of 10 m/s. Find its centripetal acceleration.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The car moves in a circle at constant speed, so it has centripetal acceleration directed toward the center.
Select a = v²/r.
Substitute v = 10 m/s, r = 25 m: a = 100/25.
Compute a = 4 m/s².

100 m/s².misconception: computed v² correctly but forgot to divide by the radius

0.25 m/s².misconception: inverted the formula, computing r/v² instead of v²/r

text: A 0.5 kg ball attached to a string moves in a horizontal circle of radius 2 m at a constant speed of 4 m/s. Find the tension in the string.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The string provides the centripetal force needed to keep the ball moving in its circular path.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying the source of centripetal force

solution_steps.step_text: Select T = mv²/r.
Substitute m = 0.5 kg, v = 4 m/s, r = 2 m: T = 0.5×16/2.
Compute T = 8/2 = 4 N.

8 N.misconception: computed mv² correctly but forgot to divide by the radius

1 N.misconception: used v instead of v² in the tension formula

16 N.misconception: multiplied by the radius instead of dividing by it

text: A solid sphere of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m rotates about an axis through its diameter. Find its moment of inertia. (For a solid sphere about its diameter, I = (2/5)MR².)
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The sphere is a standard rigid body with a known moment-of-inertia formula about its diameter.
Select I = (2/5)MR².
Substitute M = 2 kg, R = 0.5 m: I = (2/5)×2×0.25.
Compute I = 0.4×0.5 = 0.2 kg·m².

0.5 kg·m².misconception: used I = MR² as for a point mass or hoop, forgetting the 2/5 factor for a solid sphere

0.4 kg·m².misconception: used R instead of R² in the formula

0.1 kg·m².misconception: used the coefficient 1/5 instead of 2/5 for a solid sphere

text: A uniform disc of mass 4 kg and radius 0.5 m, free to rotate about its central axis, has a tangential force of 8 N applied at its rim. Find the angular acceleration produced. (For a disc about its central axis, I = ½MR².)
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: A tangential force at the rim produces a torque about the central axis, which relates to angular acceleration through the rotational analogue of Newton's second law.
Select torque τ = F×R, moment of inertia I = ½MR², and α = τ/I.
solution_steps.formula_used: τ = FR; I = ½MR²; α = τ/I

solution_steps.step_text: Substitute F = 8 N, R = 0.5 m, M = 4 kg: τ = 8×0.5 = 4 N·m. I = ½×4×0.25 = 0.5 kg·m².
solution_steps.formula_used: τ = FR; I = ½MR²; α = τ/I

solution_steps.step_text: Compute α = τ/I = 4/0.5 = 8 rad/s².

4 rad/s².misconception: used I = MR² instead of ½MR², forgetting the disc's moment-of-inertia coefficient

16 rad/s².misconception: forgot to include the radius in the torque calculation, using τ = F directly instead of τ = FR

2 rad/s².misconception: applied the translational form F = Ma instead of the rotational analogue τ = Iα

text: Find the gravitational force of attraction between two point masses of 3 kg and 4 kg placed 2 m apart. (Take G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².)
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The two point masses attract each other according to Newton's law of gravitation.
Select F = Gm1m2/r².
Substitute G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹, m1 = 3 kg, m2 = 4 kg, r = 2 m: F = 6.67×10⁻¹¹×12/4.
Compute F = 6.67×10⁻¹¹×3 ≈ 2×10⁻¹⁰ N.

4 × 10⁻¹⁰ N.misconception: used r instead of r² in the denominator

1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ N.misconception: added the two masses instead of multiplying them

3 N.misconception: omitted the gravitational constant G entirely from the formula

text: A satellite orbits the Earth at a radius equal to 4 times the Earth's radius R. Given the surface acceleration due to gravity g = 10 m/s² and R = 6.4×10⁶ m, find the orbital speed of the satellite.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: Gravity supplies the centripetal force for the satellite's circular orbit, and GM can be replaced by gR² using the surface value of g.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying orbital motion and relating GM to surface gravity

solution_steps.step_text: Select v = √(GM/r) = √(gR²/r), with orbital radius r = 4R.
Compute v = 8000/2 = 4000 m/s = 4 km/s.

8 km/s.misconception: used the surface orbital velocity √(gR) directly, without adjusting for the increased orbital radius of 4R

2 km/s.misconception: divided the surface orbital velocity by 4 instead of by √4 = 2

16 km/s.misconception: multiplied by √4 instead of dividing by it, effectively assuming orbital velocity increases with orbital radius

text: A particle executes simple harmonic motion with amplitude 5 cm and time period 2 s. Find its maximum velocity.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: In SHM, the maximum speed occurs at the mean position and depends on the angular frequency and amplitude.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying where maximum velocity occurs in SHM

solution_steps.step_text: Select ω = 2π/T and v_max = ωA.
Substitute T = 2 s: ω = 2π/2 = π rad/s. Substitute A = 5 cm: v_max = π×5.
Compute v_max = 5π cm/s.

10π cm/s.misconception: used the full peak-to-peak displacement (2A) instead of the amplitude A

2.5π cm/s.misconception: used half the amplitude by mistake instead of the full amplitude

2.5 cm/s.misconception: used ω = 1/T instead of ω = 2π/T, dropping the 2π factor

text: A 2 kg block attached to a spring of force constant 200 N/m undergoes simple harmonic motion with amplitude 0.1 m. Find its speed when its displacement from the mean position is 0.06 m.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: For a spring-block SHM system, the angular frequency depends on the spring constant and mass, and speed at any displacement follows the standard SHM speed relation.
Select ω = √(k/m) and v = ω√(A² − x²).
Compute v = 10×0.08 = 0.8 m/s.

1 m/s.misconception: used the maximum velocity formula v = ωA, ignoring the given displacement from the mean position

0.08 m/s.misconception: computed √(A²−x²) correctly but forgot to multiply by ω

8 m/s.misconception: used ω = k/m instead of ω = √(k/m)
